description: SHITTT I DON'T KNOW ANYTHING BUT WHO CARES
summary:
When a source looks brighter in a second image, did it actually change, or did the telescope observe it at a different wavelength?

We built SkyWitness, a free browser-based tool that lets anyone investigate questions like this using real observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Visitors pick a location on an interactive sky map, browse dated observations from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, and compare visits by blinking between them, viewing them side by side, or subtracting compatible images.

In Scientific Lab, visitors can measure a source’s apparent position and infrared brightness, see the uncertainty in each measurement, and download the original FITS data. Our Evidence Passport explains what the observations support in plain language and records the measurements and quality checks for closer review. In the saved Epsilon Indi B example, the two visits record different brightness values at different wavelengths, leaving a change over time inconclusive.

Pip, our interactive guide, helps beginners compare visits, read the charts, and understand why some results need more evidence. A student can start with a click on the sky and finish by explaining what two real NASA observations reveal and what evidence they would need next.
details:
A public tool for investigating changes in the sky

We built SkyWitness for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge so that anyone with a browser can compare real infrared observations and ask what changed between visits. A visitor can begin with a click on the sky and follow an investigation all the way to the measurements, their uncertainties, and the files behind them.

How it works

In Explore, visitors choose a preset target or click the Digitized Sky Survey map to fill in its sky coordinates. They can set a field of view and search the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive for SPHEREx observations, with optional date and wavelength filters.

In Observatory, a dated timeline lets visitors choose two visits and blink between them or view them side by side. Difference mode checks whether the images are compatible before subtracting them. Visitors can also download FITS cutouts containing the measured pixel values for further analysis.

In Scientific Lab, SkyWitness measures the apparent position and infrared brightness of a source from the FITS data. The Evidence Passport explains in plain language which conclusions the pair supports and why. Its advanced details and export preserve the observation identifiers, measurements, uncertainties, and quality checks so someone else can review the result.

What two real observations showed

In the saved Epsilon Indi B demonstration, Visit A measured 62.74 ± 0.47 mJy at 4.027 µm, and Visit B measured 60.82 ± 0.47 mJy at 4.062 µm. The visits sampled different wavelengths, so the difference leaves a brightness change over time inconclusive. Too few nearby reference stars lined up reliably to interpret the apparent position offset as motion. This is the judgment SkyWitness helps visitors make. They can see what the telescope measured and understand what additional evidence would help settle the question.

What we built and why it matters

We used JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Aladin Lite for the browser experience, Python and Astroquery for archive access, and Astropy for FITS analysis. We deployed SkyWitness on Vercel. We also built Pip, an animated guide that offers step-by-step explanations, points to features on the page, and uses Gemini for open-ended questions. Saved observations keep the guided investigation available during archive interruptions.

SkyWitness gives teachers a hands-on exercise with real NASA data and gives curious visitors a way to learn a skill they can apply to other repeat observations. They can spot a possible change, test whether the observations are comparable, and explain what the evidence supports.
